K-395.h1: Find 5 Differences: Dog in the Garden
K-395.title: Find 5 Differences Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-395.metaDescription: Find the differences worksheet: a dog in the garden drawn twice, five changes in picture 2. Circle them, tick five boxes. Kindergarten PDF with answer key and tap screen.
K-395.p1: A dog sits in a garden twice on this kindergarten page: picture 1 on top, picture 2 right under it, and a column of five tick boxes beside them. The two pictures are the same scene drawn from the same art, so a child's eye slides from one to the other without hunting for the matching spot. Five things are different in picture 2. On the sheet shown a butterfly has been swapped for another, a hummingbird has turned round, a cloud has grown, the flower is a different flower and the ladybug is bigger; another copy of this find-the-differences page draws its five changes afresh, so the kinds vary (something gone, something new, something bigger or smaller, something moved or flipped) while the count stays five.
K-395.p2: The task is comparison, not guessing. A child looks at one part of picture 1, finds the same part in picture 2 and decides whether it still matches. That is the visual discrimination work that later carries reading (b against d, 6 against 9) and careful looking in science, done here with a dog, clouds and flowers. The tick boxes turn the search into a count: five boxes, five finds, and the child knows when the page is done.
K-395.p3: This is the base page of the family. Its siblings change one thing each: three big differences for a first attempt, coloured pictures, seven or ten differences across two pairs, a secret count, words to tick, a mirrored picture, missing things, picture pairs and a writing page. Every version prints as a PDF, opens as a tap-the-differences screen on a tablet, and comes with an answer key that rings each change with a number. These pages compare two pictures of one scene; mirror drawing, colouring by number and finding the odd one out have pages of their own.

K-397.h1: Find 3 Big Differences: Bucket and Spade
K-397.title: Find 3 Differences Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-397.metaDescription: Find 3 differences worksheet for a first try: a beach with a bucket and spade drawn twice, three big changes, three boxes. Kindergarten PDF with answer key and screen.
K-397.p1: Three differences, each of them big: this is the page to hand a child who has never compared two pictures before. The beach scene with the bucket and spade, the ball, the starfish and two chicks is drawn twice, one picture above the other, and only three things change in the lower one. On the copy shown the sun has become a moon, a cloud has grown and one chick is much bigger; small changes such as a rotated detail are kept off this kindergarten page on purpose, so that every difference is the size of a whole object.
K-397.p2: Three is a count a four-year-old can hold in one hand, and the three large tick boxes beside the pictures match it. The child circles each change in the bottom picture and ticks a box, then looks back to check that three boxes are ticked and three rings drawn. The lesson is the method, slowly: look at one thing in the top picture, find it below, ask whether it is still the same, move on.
K-397.p3: Print the PDF for the table, or open the tap screen on a tablet where each found difference lights up; the answer key rings the three changes with numbers 1 to 3. When three big ones come easily, the base page of the find-the-differences family offers five, and the pond page seven across two pairs. These pages compare two pictures of one scene; mirror drawing, colouring by number and odd-one-out puzzles have their own pages.

K-398.h1: Find the Differences in Color: Frog at the Pond
K-398.title: Color Find the Differences Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-398.metaDescription: Find the differences in colour: a painted frog pond drawn twice, five changes, at least one a new colour. Circle and tick. Kindergarten PDF with answer key and screen.
K-398.p1: The pond is painted on this page. A green frog sits on a blue pond under a yellow sun, with a purple butterfly, hummingbirds, a red tulip and two chicks, and the whole scene appears twice. Five things differ in the coloured bottom picture, and at least one of them is a change of colour only: on the sheet shown the frog has turned purple and the butterfly orange, while a cloud has grown, a chick has turned round and the flower has become a tulip. Colour is the point of this kindergarten page, so it is printed in colour and reads best that way; on a black-and-white printer the colour change is lost and the base page serves better.
K-398.p2: Spotting that an object is the same shape in the same place but a different colour is a harder comparison than noticing something gone. The child has to hold the colour of the top frog in mind while looking at the bottom one. The five tick boxes keep the count honest, and the page asks the child to look closely at colours as well as shapes.
K-398.p3: Every page in this find-the-differences family prints as a PDF, opens as a tap screen on a tablet and comes with an answer key that rings the five changes. This is the one coloured page of the family; its siblings are line drawings. These pages compare two pictures of one scene; colouring by number uses the same scenes for a different task, and mirror drawing and odd-one-out puzzles have pages of their own.

G1-412.title: Find 7 Differences Worksheet for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-412.metaDescription: Find 7 differences worksheet: a turtle and an alligator at the pond, each scene drawn twice, four changes left, three right. Grade 1 PDF with answer key and screen.
G1-412.p1: Seven differences on one sheet, split across two pond scenes. The left pair shows a turtle by the pond with four changes between its top and bottom pictures; the right pair shows an alligator with three. Each pair has its own row of tick boxes underneath, 4 and 3, so a child who finishes one scene can see it is complete before starting the other. The four pictures share the same sky props, which is why the index tabs 1 and 2 matter: compare top with bottom inside a pair, never left with right. This grade-1 page is the seven-differences page of the find-the-differences family.
G1-412.p2: Seven is the count many European puzzle books use, and this page earns it with smaller changes than the kindergarten pages: on the copy shown a hummingbird has turned round, a butterfly is gone, a tulip has shrunk, a cloud has grown and a mushroom is smaller. The child has to scan the whole picture rather than spot the one big thing, and the two pairs mean two fresh starts on one sheet.
G1-412.p3: The PDF prints the two pairs side by side; on a tablet the tap screen stacks the four pictures with the same 1 and 2 badges and a bar between the pairs, and the answer key rings the seven changes with numbers. The ten-differences page uses the same two-pair layout for the hardest version. These pages compare two pictures of one scene; mirror drawing, colouring by number and odd-one-out puzzles have their own pages.

G2-388.title: Find 10 Differences Worksheet, Hard, for Grade 2 | Free Printable PDF
G2-388.metaDescription: Find 10 differences worksheet, the hard page: two garden scenes with a kite and a ladybug, five changes per pair. Grade 2 PDF with answer key and tap screen.
G2-388.p1: Ten differences is the hard page. Two garden scenes, one with a kite and one with a ladybug, are each drawn twice, and five things change in every pair, with a row of five tick boxes under each. The changes here are allowed to be small: a flipped bird, a slightly smaller butterfly, a cloud that moved a little, a detail gone from a drawing. A grade-2 child who found the seven-differences pond page easy is the reader this sheet is written for.
G2-388.p2: Searching for ten small changes is sustained attention work. The two-pair layout gives it a structure: finish the kite pair, tick five boxes, then start again on the ladybug pair. The numbered tabs 1 and 2 on every picture keep the comparison inside a pair, because the two scenes share the same sky and could be confused at a glance. Circling each find as it is made, before ticking, stops the common error of counting a difference twice.
G2-388.p3: The PDF prints both pairs on one sheet; the tap screen stacks the four pictures with the same badges and a bar between the pairs; the answer key rings all ten changes with numbers, five per pair, so marking takes a minute. Easier siblings in the find-the-differences family offer three, five and seven differences. These pages compare two pictures of one scene; mirror drawing, colouring by number and odd-one-out puzzles have their own pages.

G1-413.h1: How Many Differences? Count and Write the Number
G1-413.title: How Many Differences Worksheet for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-413.metaDescription: Find the differences and count them: a garden scene drawn twice, the number of changes kept secret. Circle each, write how many. Grade 1 PDF with answer key and screen.
G1-413.p1: Nobody tells the child how many differences there are. A garden scene with a chick, a hummingbird, a butterfly, flowers and a ladybug is drawn twice, and the only ledger on the page is a single empty box for a numeral. The child circles every change found in the bottom picture, including places where something has simply gone, and then writes the total. On the copy shown that total is six, but every printed copy of this grade-1 page draws its own number of changes, so the count is a genuine secret.
G1-413.p2: This turns comparison into counting. Finding the changes is the visual work; keeping a running tally of circles and writing the numeral is the counting work, the kind a first grader is asked to do with sets of objects. Because the instruction says that something may be gone, an empty space counts as a find, which stops children from reporting only the changes that are still visible.
G1-413.p3: The answer key rings every change and prints the number in the box; the tap screen asks the child to tap each difference and then choose the right numeral from a row of four, 3 to 6. The base page of the find-the-differences family tells the count outright, which is the version to use first. These pages compare two pictures of one scene; mirror drawing, colouring by number and odd-one-out puzzles have their own pages.

G1-414.title: What Changed? Tick the Words Worksheet for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-414.metaDescription: Find the differences and name them: a farm scene drawn twice, three changes, six picture words. Circle the changes, tick the words. Grade 1 PDF with answer key.
G1-414.p1: Next to the two farm pictures stands a column of six words: hummingbird, butterfly, hay, sun, cloud, barn. Three things are different in the bottom picture, and after circling them the child ticks the words of the things that changed. The words are the real vocabulary of the picture, and three of the six are decoys that name things which stayed the same. On this grade-1 sheet, written for the find-the-differences family, the reading load is six nouns and nothing more.
G1-414.p2: Matching a change to its word is the bridge from looking to language. A child who has found that the sun is gone must then decide that the word for it is sun, not cloud. The page never offers two words for one drawing, so each tick has one right answer: where a picture holds both a generic bird and a named one, only the specific word is listed. Decoy words make the ticking a decision rather than a habit.
G1-414.p3: The answer key rings the three changes and ticks the three right words; the tap screen asks the child to tap the changes and then tap the words. Its sibling, Write What Is Different, moves the same idea into sentences for second graders. These pages compare two pictures of one scene; mirror drawing, colouring by number and odd-one-out puzzles have their own pages.

G1-415.h1: Mirror Pictures: Find the Differences, Then Fold to Check
G1-415.title: Mirror Find the Differences Worksheet for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-415.metaDescription: Find the differences in a mirrored picture: a fox in the forest, picture 2 flipped, four real changes. Fold on the line to check. Grade 1 PDF with answer key.
G1-415.p1: Picture 2 on this page is flipped like a mirror. A fox in the forest appears on the left, and its mirror image sits on the right with a dashed fold line between them. The flip itself is not a difference: four things are still changed inside the mirrored picture, and they may be a thing that is gone, something swapped, something bigger or smaller. Four tick boxes sit under picture 2. When the child has circled four things, folding the page along the line lays one picture over the other, and holding it to the light shows where they disagree. This is the grade-1 mirror page of the find-the-differences family.
G1-415.p2: Comparing a scene with its mirror image asks a child to map left to right in the head, the same move that tells b from d and p from q. Everything is in the expected place once the flip is understood; the four real changes are hidden inside that extra step. The fold is the self-check, so the page marks itself before an adult sees it.
G1-415.p3: The answer key rings the four changes and ticks the boxes; the tap screen shows the two pictures stacked with the lower one mirrored and asks the child to tap each real change. These pages compare two pictures of one scene; the symmetry pages, where a child draws the other half of a picture, and colouring by number have pages of their own.

K-399.h1: What Is Missing? Circle the Empty Place
K-399.title: What Is Missing Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-399.metaDescription: What is missing worksheet: a night scene with an owl drawn twice, three things gone. Circle the empty places, tick three boxes. Kindergarten PDF with answer key.
K-399.p1: Nothing is swapped, moved or resized on this page: things simply disappear. An owl sits under the moon with stars, planets and mushrooms in picture 1, and in picture 2 three of those things are gone, leaving empty places in the night sky and on the ground. The child circles the three empty places and ticks three boxes. Only removal is used on this kindergarten version, so the question stays one question: what was there, and is it still there?
K-399.p2: Noticing absence is harder than noticing a change, because there is nothing to look at where the thing used to be. The child has to remember the top picture while scanning the bottom one, which is the memory part of visual comparison. Three items keep it within reach of a five-year-old, and the circle drawn around empty paper is a satisfying answer to write.
K-399.p3: The answer key rings the three empty places with numbers; the tap screen asks the child to tap each empty place in the lower picture. The base page of the find-the-differences family mixes all the kinds of change, which is the step after this one. These pages compare two pictures of one scene; mirror drawing, colouring by number and odd-one-out puzzles have their own pages.

K-400.h1: Picture Pairs: One Difference in Every Row
K-400.title: Picture Pairs Find the Difference Worksheet | Free Printable PDF
K-400.metaDescription: Picture pairs worksheet: three rows of garden close-ups shown twice, one difference per row. Circle it, tick the box. Kindergarten PDF with answer key and screen.
K-400.p1: Instead of one big scene, this page cuts a garden into three close-ups and shows each of them twice, side by side in a row. In every row exactly one thing is different in the right-hand picture, and a tick box ends the row. The windows are large and the objects few, so a child can take one row at a time: on the copy shown a hummingbird has grown in the first row, the sun is gone from the second and a chick is bigger in the third. The find-the-differences idea arrives here in its smallest, calmest form for kindergarten.
K-400.p2: One difference per row removes the question of when to stop. The child compares two small pictures, finds the single change, circles it, ticks the box and moves down. Because a difference may be something gone, the instruction asks for the place that is different rather than the thing, and a circle around an empty patch of paper is a right answer.
K-400.p3: The answer key rings each change; the tap screen stacks the two pictures of a row and asks the child to tap the one place that differs. From here the three-differences and five-differences pages of the family put the comparison back into one whole scene. These pages compare two pictures of one scene; mirror drawing, colouring by number and odd-one-out puzzles have their own pages.

G2-389.h1: Write What Is Different: One Sentence per Difference
G2-389.title: Write What Is Different Worksheet for Grade 2 | Free Printable PDF
G2-389.metaDescription: Find the differences and write about them: an elephant scene drawn twice, three changes, word strips and three sentence lines. Grade 2 PDF with answer key.
G2-389.p1: Two pictures of an elephant under a tree sit side by side, with three changes between them, and under them run two word strips: six nouns from the picture (tree, elephant, bird, sun, flower, cloud) and seven change words (missing, bigger, smaller, moved, flipped, new, changed). Three ruled lines each begin with the printed starter In picture 2, and the child completes one sentence per difference by taking a noun from the first strip and a change word from the second. This grade-2 page is the writing page of the find-the-differences family.
G2-389.p2: Describing a difference in a sentence makes the child name both the thing and what happened to it: In picture 2, the cloud is missing. The strips supply the spelling so the effort goes into the comparison and the sentence, not into guessing letters. A difference may be something that is gone, which is why the word missing is on the strip and the instruction says so.
G2-389.p3: The answer key rings the three changes with numbers; the tap screen asks the child to tap the differences before writing. Its sibling What Changed? Tick the Words asks for the same judgement with ticks instead of sentences, a year earlier. These pages compare two pictures of one scene; picture writing, mirror drawing and colouring by number have pages of their own.

K-396.h1: How to Draw a Cat Step by Step
K-396.title: How to Draw a Cat Step by Step Worksheet | Free Printable PDF
K-396.metaDescription: How to draw a cat step by step: four numbered steps down the side, the new lines of each step in orange, and a big dashed paper to draw on. Kindergarten PDF.
K-396.p1: Four numbered steps run down the left of this page, and the rest of it is one big dashed paper. Step 1 is the cat's outline on its own, drawn in orange; in steps 2 and 3 the earlier lines are black and the new lines are orange, so a child can see exactly what is added each time; step 4 shows the finished cat. The steps are cut from the drawing itself, not redrawn, which is why the cat on the card and the cat the child is aiming for are the same cat. This is the base page of the how-to-draw family for kindergarten.
K-396.p2: Drawing from steps teaches a child to see a whole animal as an outline plus parts added in order, which is how confident drawers work and the opposite of starting with an eye and running out of room. Keeping the child's drawing on a large paper beside the small steps also trains looking from a model to a page, a skill that writing will need.
K-396.p3: Print it on plain paper and give the child a pencil; nothing else is needed, and there is no answer to mark because the drawing is the child's own. The family's ten other pages change one thing each: dotted shapes to start from, a grey cat-sized model to trace, an unfinished copy to complete, a grid, a word to write, a scene, mixed-up steps, a box for every step, three sentences, and drawing from memory. The child draws the animal from its own steps; tracing letters, grid-copy pixels and symmetry drawing have their own pages.

K-401.h1: Draw a Dog with Simple Shapes
K-401.title: Draw a Dog with Simple Shapes Worksheet | Free Printable PDF
K-401.metaDescription: Draw a dog from simple shapes: four dotted ovals on the paper for the head, ears and body, four numbered steps beside it. Kindergarten printable PDF.
K-401.p1: The big paper on this page is not empty. Four dotted shapes already sit on it, an oval for the head, one for each ear and a tall oval for the body, placed exactly where the dog's parts go. The child goes over the dotted shapes, draws the dog's outline around them and then adds the face, legs and tail from the four numbered steps on the left. On the cards the dog grows from outline to finished drawing with the new lines of each step in orange, the same way as on every how-to-draw page for kindergarten.
K-401.p2: Shapes first is the oldest drawing lesson there is: a head is a circle, a body an oval, and the outline follows. Seeing the dotted ovals under the finished dog shows a child where a drawing comes from, and it quietly links drawing to the shape names of early geometry. Because the shapes fix the size and position, the dog comes out large and whole instead of cramped in a corner.
K-401.p3: Print it and draw with a pencil; there is nothing to mark. The base page of the family gives the same cat-sized paper with nothing on it, and the trace page gives a grey model to draw over. The child draws the animal from its own steps; tracing letters, grid-copy pixels and symmetry drawing have their own pages.

K-402.h1: Trace a Rabbit, Then Draw It Yourself
K-402.title: Trace Then Draw a Rabbit Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-402.metaDescription: Trace then draw a rabbit: a large grey rabbit to go over with a pencil, an empty box for your own rabbit, four steps across the top. Kindergarten PDF.
K-402.p1: Two boxes share this page. The left one holds a large rabbit printed in pale grey, ready to be traced with a pencil; the right one is empty, for the child's own rabbit drawn afterwards. Across the top run the four steps, outline first, with the new lines of each step in orange. Tracing the grey rabbit teaches the hand the route round the ears and the paws; drawing it again beside, without the grey, is the kindergarten child's first drawing from memory of the shape just traced.
K-402.p2: The two boxes are the same size on purpose, so the second rabbit has room to be as big as the first. Tracing a whole animal is a different exercise from tracing letters: the lines curve, cross and loop, and the pencil has to keep a steady pressure for a long run. Doing it once with help and once without is the whole method of this how-to-draw page.
K-402.p3: Print it on plain paper; the grey model prints as a light tone on any printer and there is nothing to mark. The next page of the family removes the grey model and offers dotted shapes instead; the finish page offers a half-drawn horse. The child draws the animal from its own steps; letter tracing, grid-copy pixels and symmetry drawing have their own pages.

K-403.title: Finish the Drawing Worksheet: a Horse for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-403.metaDescription: Finish the drawing: a complete horse beside the same horse missing its mane, face and leg lines. Draw what is missing, then your own horse. Kindergarten PDF.
K-403.p1: A whole horse stands on the left of this page, and on the right stands the same horse unfinished: its outline and eyes are there, but the mane, the face lines, the hooves and the lines of the legs and tail are missing. A small ring badge marks the unfinished one. The child looks from the complete horse to the incomplete one, draws in what is missing, and then draws a horse of their own on the big paper below. There is no mirror line and no half picture here; this kindergarten page is about comparing two drawings of the same horse.
K-403.p2: Finding what is missing and drawing it is observation and drawing in one move. The child must look at the finished model part by part, which teaches the parts of the animal, and then produce the lines in the right place, which teaches control. The third box lets the child try the whole horse once the parts are familiar.
K-403.p3: Print it and draw with a pencil; nothing is marked. The missing lines are chosen so that the gap is obvious to a child, and the ring and dot badges simply tell the two horses apart. The base page of the how-to-draw family gives the full four steps instead of a model to complete. The child draws the animal from its own steps; symmetry drawing, where half a picture is mirrored, and grid-copy pixels have their own pages.

G1-416.h1: Draw a Dinosaur with the Grid
G1-416.title: Grid Drawing Worksheet: Draw a Dinosaur for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-416.metaDescription: Draw a dinosaur with the grid: the dinosaur on a 4 by 4 grid, an empty grid to copy square by square, a plain box to draw it again. Grade 1 PDF.
G1-416.p1: A dinosaur stands on a four-by-four grid at the top left of this page. Beside it is an empty grid of the same size, and below both is a plain dashed box. The child copies the dinosaur into the empty grid one square at a time, looking at where the lines cross each square, and then draws it once more in the box without any grid. The grid is a drawing aid, not a pixel puzzle: lines, not filled squares, which is what separates this grade-1 page from the grid-copy pages.
G1-416.p2: Working square by square breaks a hard drawing into sixteen easy ones and teaches a child to look at position: the head is in the top left square, the tail reaches the right edge in the third row. The second drawing, without the grid, is where that looking pays off, because the child now knows the dinosaur's proportions from having measured them.
G1-416.p3: Print it on plain paper; nothing is marked, and the plain box is intentionally about the size of the grid so the second dinosaur can match the first. The base page of the how-to-draw family uses numbered steps instead of a grid. The child draws the animal from its own steps or squares; grid-copy pixel pictures, letter tracing and symmetry drawing have their own pages.

K-404.h1: Draw a Fish and Write the Word
K-404.title: Draw a Fish and Write the Word Worksheet | Free Printable PDF
K-404.metaDescription: Draw a fish from four steps, then write the word fish on the handwriting line below: trace it, then copy it once more. Kindergarten printable PDF.
K-404.p1: Under the drawing paper on this page run three handwriting lines: the word fish printed as a model, the same word in dotted grey letters to trace, and an empty line to write it alone. The four steps across the top show the fish from its outline to its finished scales, with the new lines of each step in orange. The child draws the fish on the big paper and then writes its name below: one picture, one word, both made by the child. This kindergarten page joins the how-to-draw family to the first weeks of writing.
K-404.p2: Drawing a thing and then writing its word is how early vocabulary and handwriting support each other. The word is short and the letters are the ones a kindergarten child meets first; the tracing copy is seated on the line so the letter height is right before the child writes freely. The fish drawn above gives the word a meaning the child has just made.
K-404.p3: Print it on plain paper and use a pencil for both the drawing and the word; nothing is marked. The base page of the family is the same drawing without the word line; the bear page asks for three sentences instead of one word. The child draws the animal from its own steps; letter tracing pages, grid-copy pixels and symmetry drawing have their own pages.

G1-417.h1: Draw a Frog at the Pond
G1-417.title: Draw a Frog at the Pond Worksheet for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-417.metaDescription: Draw a frog into a scene: four steps across the top, then a pond picture with a cloud, a sun and a tulip, and an empty pond for the frog. Grade 1 PDF.
G1-417.p1: The paper on this page is already a picture. A cloud and a sun sit in the sky, a tulip grows on the bank, and the pond in the middle is empty. Across the top, four numbered steps show how to draw a frog, outline first and then the eyes, legs and spots with each step's new lines in orange. The child practises the frog from the steps and then draws it on the empty pond, so the finished page is a scene rather than an animal floating on white paper. This is the grade-1 scene page of the how-to-draw family.
G1-417.p2: Placing a drawing inside a picture asks for a decision the plain pages do not: how big should the frog be, and where exactly does it sit on the pond? Children who can draw an animal often cannot yet place it, and a prepared scene with one obvious empty place teaches that placement without words. The sun, cloud and tulip also give the frog a scale to match.
G1-417.p3: Print it on plain paper; nothing is marked. The props are drawn from the same picture library as the find-the-differences pond pages, so the frog page and those pages can sit in one lesson. The base page of the family gives an empty paper instead of a scene. The child draws the animal from its own steps; letter tracing, grid-copy pixels and symmetry drawing have their own pages.

G1-418.h1: Order the Steps: Drawing an Owl
G1-418.title: Order the Steps Drawing Worksheet: an Owl for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-418.metaDescription: Order the drawing steps: five cards of an owl shuffled out of order, a box beside each for the numbers 1 to 5, then draw the owl. Grade 1 PDF.
G1-418.p1: Five cards show an owl at five stages of being drawn, and they are printed in the wrong order. Beside each card is an empty box. The child works out which card comes first, which next, and writes 1 to 5 in the boxes before drawing the owl on the paper below. The clue is in the colours: on every card the lines already drawn are black and the lines just added are orange, so the card whose orange lines are black on another card comes before it. This grade-1 page is the ordering page of the how-to-draw family.
G1-418.p2: Putting steps in order is sequencing, the same thinking as ordering the frames of a story, applied to a drawing procedure. The first and last cards are easy to spot, the all-orange outline and the finished owl, and the three in the middle need the comparison the colours make possible. A child who has ordered the cards has understood why the steps go that way, which is more than copying them.
G1-418.p3: Print it on plain paper; the finished owl on the last card is the check, every line it shows must have come in order, and the drawing is not marked. The child draws the animal from its own steps; story sequencing pages, letter tracing and grid-copy pixels have pages of their own.

G1-419.h1: Copy Each Step: Draw a Bird
G1-419.title: Copy Each Step Drawing Worksheet: a Bird for Grade 1 | Free Printable PDF
G1-419.metaDescription: Copy each drawing step: four cards of a hummingbird, an empty box under every card to copy it, and a bigger paper for the whole bird. Grade 1 PDF.
G1-419.p1: Every step on this page has its own box. Four cards across the top show a hummingbird growing from its outline to its wings and feathers, and directly under each card is an empty box the same size, so the child copies step 1, then step 2 with its new lines added, and so on. The bigger paper at the bottom is for the whole bird, drawn larger once all four steps have been practised. The grade-1 how-to-draw page that gives the most guided practice is this one.
G1-419.p2: Copying each step separately makes the child draw the outline four times and the added lines in order, which fixes the sequence far better than looking at the steps once and drawing the finished bird. The small boxes keep each attempt short; the large paper at the end asks for the same drawing at a new size, which tests whether the proportions have been learned rather than traced by eye.
G1-419.p3: Print it on plain paper; nothing is marked. The animal is a hummingbird, named bird on the page because that is the word a child uses for it. The base page of the family shows the same kind of steps with one big paper only. The child draws the animal from its own steps; letter tracing, grid-copy pixels and symmetry drawing have their own pages.

G2-390.h1: Draw a Bear, Then Write About It
G2-390.title: Draw and Write Worksheet: a Bear for Grade 2 | Free Printable PDF
G2-390.metaDescription: Draw a bear from four steps, then write three sentences about it on ruled lines that begin My bear is, It can and It likes. Grade 2 how-to-draw and writing printable PDF.
G2-390.p1: The four steps of a bear run down the left of this page, outline first with each step's new lines in orange, and the big paper for the drawing sits beside them. Under the paper are three ruled handwriting lines, each starting with printed words: My bear is, It can, It likes. The child draws the bear and then finishes the three sentences about the bear just drawn. Drawing comes first on this grade-2 page, which is what separates it from picture-writing pages where the picture is given.
G2-390.p2: Writing about a drawing the child has made gives the sentences a subject the child already cares about and knows every detail of. The starters fix the sentence shapes, a description, an ability and a liking, so the writing work is in the predicate: My bear is brown and big. It can climb a tree. It likes honey. Three sentences about one character is a small piece of narrative description.
G2-390.p3: Print it on plain paper; the drawing is not marked and the sentences are read, not scored. The fish page of the how-to-draw family asks for one word where this page asks for three sentences. The child draws the animal from its own steps; picture writing from a given picture, letter tracing and grid-copy pixels have pages of their own.

G2-391.title: Draw from Memory Worksheet: a Butterfly for Grade 2 | Free Printable PDF
G2-391.metaDescription: Draw a butterfly from memory: a small butterfly on a flap, a dashed fold line and a big paper below. Look, fold the model away, draw it. Grade 2 PDF.
G2-391.p1: A small butterfly sits on a cream flap at the top of this page, a dashed line runs across under it, and the rest of the sheet is one big paper. The child looks at the butterfly for as long as they like, folds the top of the page back along the dashed line so the model is out of sight, and draws the butterfly from memory. Unfolding the page afterwards puts the model and the drawing side by side. This grade-2 page is the memory page of the how-to-draw family and has no steps at all.
G2-391.p2: Drawing from memory asks a child to study a picture with a purpose, which is a different kind of looking from copying. The questions come naturally while the model is still visible: how many wings, where do the antennae start, is the body long or short? A symmetrical animal is a fair first subject, because remembering one wing gives the other.
G2-391.p3: Print it on plain paper and fold along the line; there is nothing to mark, and comparing the drawing with the model after unfolding is the whole review. The base page of the family shows the steps in full for a child who is not ready to draw unaided. The child draws the animal from its own observation; symmetry drawing, letter tracing and grid-copy pixels have their own pages.
